title: Fisheries of the Caribbean, Gulf of America, and South Atlantic; Fishery Management Plans of Puerto Rico, St. Croix, and St. Thomas and St. John; Amendment 2
summary:
Big changes just landed in two very different corners of federal policy: the government is tightening how it decides which companies qualify as “disadvantaged” for contracting, and it’s adding new gear rules to protect fish and habitats in U.S. Caribbean waters. There’s also a temporary extension of catch limits for the Northeast groundfish fleet so the season can continue while longer-term measures are finished.

On federal contracting, every business that wants to be counted as “socially and economically disadvantaged” will now have to prove it through a personal narrative and financial details based on their own experiences—not by relying on race or sex. States that certify these firms must reevaluate every current certification. Until that reevaluation is done, agencies can’t set contract goals tied to disadvantaged participation or count those awards toward goals. Supporters say this raises the bar, reduces abuse, and focuses help on those who can show real barriers and economic harm. But many certified firms could face uncertainty or lose eligibility, and agencies and primes may see delays and added paperwork as certifications are revisited.

In the Caribbean, the federal fisheries agency is taking a precautionary path to protect reefs and reduce unintended catch. Trawls, trammel nets, and purse seines are now off-limits in federal waters around Puerto Rico, St. Croix, and St. Thomas and St. John. Gillnets are banned for managed species and allowed only in limited ways for non-managed bait fishing, with strict size, depth, and tending rules. Starting April 1, 2026, boats fishing for reef fish must also have a simple weighted tool on board to quickly return released fish to depth, improving their chance of survival after being brought up from deeper water. Conservation groups and future fishers stand to gain from healthier habitats and stocks, and many boats won’t see big changes because these nets were rarely used offshore. Still, some fishermen will need to adjust practices, buy or make devices, and comply with new limits that can feel restrictive in the short term.

Finally, for the Northeast groundfish fishery, emergency measures are extended through April 30, 2026. That keeps interim catch limits and certain possession bans in place for species like cod and haddock so the fishery can keep operating while preventing overfishing. This helps boats and coastal communities avoid a shutdown, but some operators remain constrained by low quotas and the uncertainty that comes with stopgap rules.
